title: This Is Why We Run Trials, Unfortunately
body_text: Inflammation is one of those huge topics in medicine that you really can’t seem to escape. The immune system is constantly at work - well, it had better be - monitoring for signs of infection and damage and responding to these through a bewildering number of pathways. It’s become apparent over the decades, though, that the immune response is not only a double-edged sword, but that it might well be larger, sharper, and swinging around more constantly than we realized. You can see this most vividly in the recognized autoimmune disorders like lupus, arthritis, Hashimoto’s, multiple sclerosis and more, which are a flagrant attack on the body’s own tissues. But less-obvious long-running inflammation is widely thought to be a contributor (and perhaps even a root cause) of many other conditions, particularly with aging. It’s a drain on the body’s resources to keep these fights going, and it appears to cause all kinds of slow, inexorable damage along the way. But what to do about that? The entire evolutionary story of the immune system is walking that line between benefit and damage, between doing too little and doing too much. The biological systems we see are the result, and one big part of it is that selection pressure is strongest by far during the childbearing years when genes are passed on to another generation. Having a system that protects your body vigorously in your early decades but gradually goes awry if your lifespan stretches out enough isn’t really much of a problem. And that’s true even if some of those earlier protections are a bit too vigorous or go off the rails once in a while, just so long as having the system working at that level provides more benefit most of the time. That seems to be the situation we’re in - but more people are living longer lifespans and the entire story of medical science is that we don’t necessarily have to take the hand that we’re dealt by nature. And there are many therapies that have been developed in that way for inflammation and immune response. A lot of the time in this field you find yourself working with antibody therapies, because the various signaling networks are not necessarily driven by small-molecule binding sites at their receptors, activating or inactivating enzymes, etc. If you look at the list of highest-selling prescription drugs, you find antibodies that block interleukin-4 and interleukin 13, or block IL-23A, or block IL-23A and IL-12, or block tumor necrosis factor, and that’s just the beginning. Novo Nordisk has been trying to add to that list with ziltivekimab, which targets interleukin-6. Like a lot of these targets, IL-6 has a very wide range of actions. Just look at that last link, where the biological functions just keep going and going - metabolic, immune, CNS, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, aging in general. Novo was building on a large body of evidence that elevated IL-6 is associated with all kinds of cardiovascular risk (heart attack and heart failure in general, stroke, artery disease, you name it). These associations have shown up in multiple studies in many different populations, and human genetic studies indicate that lowering IL-6 activity is associated with lower cardiovascular risk. So a direct pharmacological shot at IL-6 activity like this one has been highly anticipated. (As an aside, I have no idea if there were any bets on this one on the prediction markets I wrote about yesterday. . .) Well, you see where this is going. A large trial (ZEUS) just read out a few days ago, and yes, ziltivekimab did indeed lower IL-6 in the treated patients as well as lowered markers of inflammation like C-reactive protein. This was in a patient population that had high levels of both and had heart or kidney disease already, and the thinking was that these people would be the best group to show benefits from IL-6 inhibition. But that simply didn’t happen. Cardiovascular events and deaths were no different from the control group. A higher number of people in the treatment group came down with serious infections - which is what you always have to expect when you’re dialing back the immune system - but all-causes mortality was the same in both the treatment group and the placebo controls. This really makes a person wonder about the whole cardiovascular inflammation idea. Novo Nordisk has another ongoing trial in patients with heart failure, and a third in people who have already had a heart attack, but after these results, it’ll be another major surprise if either of those are encouraging. As this New York Times article notes, there have been occasional puzzling results over the years in connecting inflammation with cardiovascular disease, but this is by far the biggest hit the hypothesis has ever taken. Maybe these patients were too far long in the disease process to be helped? That’s a worry with designing trials in any chronic condition, of course (as see the never-ending arguments about Alzheimer’s trial results). Or maybe the connection between chronic inflammation and cardiac events is a lot more complicated than we realized. Sadly, that point of view is often a winner in this business.
